Chapter 5: Common Objections and the Power of Optimism Bias
When you first hear the idea that simply coming into existence could actually be a harm, it’s natural to feel a wave of disbelief—or even a bit of anger. After all, the belief that life is inherently good runs deep. Questioning that can feel almost like challenging something sacred. So, it’s no surprise that people come up with all kinds of objections, trying to defend the value of existence and the morality behind choosing to bring new life into the world.
One of the most common responses? People bring up the joys of life—love, friendship, those moments of achievement, and the beauty we experience. The argument goes, “These pleasures make everything worthwhile. Sure, there’s pain, but isn't it a price worth paying?”
But here’s something to pay attention to: there’s an important asymmetry between pain and pleasure. If someone never exists, the absence of pleasure isn’t a loss for them. But for someone who does exist, any pain they experience is always a harm.
Another objection you’ll often hear is, “Life is what you make of it. If you’re unhappy, try to change things—find meaning or focus on the positive.” It’s well-meaning advice, and it sounds empowering, right? But this actually misses the heart of the question. It’s not about whether people can handle suffering once they’re here. It’s about whether it’s right to bring someone into the world, knowing there will be suffering—before they even have a chance to choose.
Some folks say suffering is necessary for growth. It builds character, and resilience, and helps us learn. But think about it: this really only makes sense for people who already exist. It doesn’t explain why we should create someone, knowing they’ll suffer, just so they get the chance to grow from it. The harm that comes with existence isn’t justified simply by the possibility of growth or achievement.
There’s also a tendency to brush off the harm of existence by saying, “Well, most people are happy to be alive.” But here’s where psychology steps in. We humans are incredibly good at adapting. We find meaning even in hardship, and we have this built-in optimism bias—convincing ourselves that life is better than it really is. This optimism bias helps us get by, but it doesn’t necessarily tell us the true value of existence.
Picture a group of friends sitting around a table, deep in conversation. Some are convinced life is a gift, that the good times outweigh the bad. Others are more cautious—they recognize the suffering, but still believe life is worth living. And a few sit quietly, bothered by the idea that bringing someone into existence could actually be a harm.
As the discussion goes on, you can sense that most people would rather focus on the good—on the blessings—than really face the reality of suffering. But those doubts? They’re still there, just beneath the surface. Optimism bias is powerful, but it can’t erase the real harm that sometimes comes with simply being alive.
So, when everyone leaves the table, each person carries their own mix of comfort and unease. For some, their beliefs are reassuring. For others, the questions stick with them, unsettled. The conversation lingers—a reminder that the value of existence isn’t as simple, or as certain, as it might seem.
